claim: A 2025 IRT reanalysis of the GJP data found that extraneous variables eliminated, reduced or reversed the teaming and training effects reported by Mellers et al. 2014.
quote: substantially eliminated, reduced, and, in some cases, even reversed the effects of the experimental manipulations of teaming and training on latent forecasting ability
title: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting: The Effect of Uncontrolled Method Variance on Statistical Conclusions
n: first 2 years of the GJP tournament
transfer: Do not treat the human 'training raises skill' result as proof for base-rate or decomposition steps. Each step must pass our own equal-token test.

claim: The same reanalysis says traits tied to strategic responding separate superforecasters from others, so the cause of their edge is hard to identify.
quote: latent traits associated with strategic responding can discriminate between superforecasters and non-superforecasters
title: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting
transfer: Superforecaster habits may be partly response strategy (how people use the 0-1 scale), not thinking. Score the agent on outcomes, not on whether it follows the habit list.

claim: The earlier brief lists the reanalysis author order wrongly; the page gives Hauenstein, Thomas, Illingworth, Dougherty.
title: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting

claim: Reasoning models are typically overconfident, often stating over 85% confidence when wrong, and confidence gets worse as reasoning gets deeper.
authors: Mei, Zhang, Yin, Lidard, Shorinwa, Majumdar
title: Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
transfer: Do not trust a stated confidence after a long chain of thought. Use sample agreement or a check result for stop rules.

claim: Asking a model to review its own reasoning to judge its answer (introspective UQ) helped o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 but made Claude 3.7 Sonnet worse calibrated.
authors: Mei, Zhang, Yin, Lidard, Shorinwa, Majumdar
title: Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
transfer: A self-review calibration step can backfire per model. Gate it on a measured gain for our model, never assume.

claim: Reasoning models were better calibrated than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings, and removing slow-thinking behaviours (backtracking, trying alternatives) reduced calibration. This conflicts with c-04.
authors: Yoon, Kim, Yang, Kim, Kim, Kim, Choi, Kim, Seo
title: Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
transfer: The evidence on whether long reasoning helps calibration is split. Measure it on our model; do not hard-wire either belief.

claim: Reasoning-trained models say 'I don't know' much less on factuality tasks and show higher confidence when reasoning is shorter; the authors name a possible 'reasoning tax' on knowing one's limits, mainly in small models.
quote: reasoning models may possess a diminished awareness of their own knowledge boundaries
title: Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?
venue: arXiv 2504.06564 (EMNLP 2025 per earlier brief, not re-checked)
transfer: On factual or lookup questions, do not let a reasoning call decide to answer vs abstain alone. Add an agreement or retrieval check.

claim: Black-box confidence methods for LLMs are overconfident when verbalising, no single technique wins consistently, and all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
quote: LLMs tend to be overconfident when verbalizing confidence
authors: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He, Hooi
title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
transfer: Use several weak signals (agreement + verbalised) and tune per task type; expect poor signal on hard expert items.

claim: Verbalised confidence beat token probabilities for RLHF models and often roughly halved calibration error, on three QA sets only (TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA). The gain is relative to a weak baseline, not proof of good calibration.
authors: Tian, Mitchell, Zhou, Sharma, Rafailov, Yao, Finn, Manning
title: Just Ask for Calibration
transfer: Verbalised confidence is usable as one input to routing but must be re-measured on our suites (ECE or AUROC).

claim: Self-evaluation on open-ended tasks needs candidate answers first, and P(IK) calibration is weak on new tasks.
title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
transfer: A 'do I know this' pre-check before attempting is unreliable on new task types; rate the answer after attempting.

claim: LLM crowd of 12 models matched 925 humans on only 31 binary questions, with a clear upward bias above 50% while resolutions were near even.
quote: Mean LLM predictions were significantly above 50%
title: Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
transfer: Check yes/high bias in any agent probability output; subtract a measured bias offset in code. Tiny question set limits trust.

claim: Showing models the human median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17-28%, but plain averaging of human and machine forecasts was more accurate. Feeding in a crowd number is worse than averaging.
quote: simply averaging human and machine forecasts was more accurate
title: Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
transfer: Combine in code (average a model probability with an external anchor) instead of showing the anchor in the prompt.

claim: On ForecastBench, expert forecasters beat the top LLM with p<0.001; the benchmark uses only unresolved questions to avoid leakage. Leaked-answer retrodiction scores should be treated as inflated.
quote: expert forecasters outperform the top-performing LLM
authors: Karger, Bastani, Yueh-Han, Jacobs, Halawi, Zhang, Tetlock
title: ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
transfer: Test any agent forecasting step only on questions that resolve after the model cutoff.

claim: Halawi et al. system came close to aggregated human forecasts and only in some settings beat them; the near-human claim rests on a retrieval, reasoning and ensembling pipeline, not on prompting alone.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
transfer: Gains came from retrieval and ensembling; a pure thinking schema without new information should expect less.

claim: LLM forecasters give logically inconsistent probabilities across related questions; the arbitrage-based inconsistency score correlates with later Brier score.
authors: Paleka, Sudhir, Alvarez, Bhat, Shen, Wang, Tramer
title: Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
transfer: Cheap check step: ask P(A), P(not A), P(A and B) in separate calls and test coherence in code; flag incoherence as low confidence.

claim: The extremizing paper in the earlier brief (arXiv 1501.06943) is marked withdrawn and superseded by 1406.2148 (Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity). The optimal extremizing amount depends on how much forecasters' information overlaps.
title: Modeling Probability Forecasts via Information Diversity
transfer: Extremize factor must shrink toward 1 as overlap rises; samples from one model overlap almost fully, so default factor 1.

claim: Project data: a scaffold that forced extra steps hurt single-answer tasks, so superforecaster-style procedures need a gate. No source was found this session that tests forecasting procedures on LLMs at equal tokens (web search budget ran out).
title: 00_PLAN.md
transfer: Gate base-rate and decomposition steps to quantity or probability questions only.
